newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Debut Eurobond strengthens Kazakh tenge, dealers.
newsitem.headline: Debut Eurobond strengthens Kazakh tenge, dealers.

text.p: Kazakh officials were all smiles on Tuesday after its debut Eurobond netted the oil-rich Central Asian nation double the planned $100 million issue and strengthened its embattled currency.
The $200 million three-year bond, organised by Dutch bank ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, was priced to yield 9.3 percent or 350 basis points above comparable U.S. Treasury notes.
"This is Kazakhstan's first step on to the international (debt) market," Finance Minister Alexander Pavlov told a news conference in the Kazakh capital Almaty.
Officials say the bond was issued not so much to raise cash but to put the remote former Soviet republic on the world financial map, the second such republic after Russia to do so.

But Pavlov said the money had already been earmarked to pay a backlog of unpaid salaries, pensions and social services in the cash-strapped state whose 16.9 million population are fast losing patience with the hardships brought by market reforms.
Dealers at Kazakh banks said the issue would temporarily strengthen the Kazakh currency, the tenge, which had fallen sharply against the dollar in recent days.
The tenge rose to 73.4855 against the dollar on Tuesday on the Kazakhstan Currency Exchange from 73.7094 on Monday.
"The inflow of cash from the bond will strengthen the tenge for a while but only temporarily," said a dealer from Kazakhstan's AO Alem Bank.

There was an air of disappointment last month when Kazakhstan achieved credit ratings slightly below those of neighbouring Russia. The rating was affected largely by Russia's continued grip on the republic's oil wealth.

Billions of dollars worth of oil and gas, on which Kazakhstan's long-term prospects depend, are locked up for lack of export alternatives to the limited capacity through pipelines belonging to Russia, its former colonial overlord.
Moody's gave the republic a Ba3 sovereign ceiling for long-term foreign currency bonds. Rating agencies IBCA and Standard and Poor's both gave Kazakhstan BB-.

A western economist based in the republic said the Russia factor had greatly influenced the Kazakh bond's pricing. "The spread is similar to Russia's which means investors do not distinguish it from Russia," he said.

But such fears apparently did not worry major institutional investors in London and New York, who snapped up nearly 80 percent of the issue, according to Pavlov. The remaining 20 percent was bought by investors in Asia.

"We've had incredible interest from investors in the Kazakh debt market following the (Eurobond) issue," said Aidan Karibzhanov, deputy managing director of Almaty-based brokers Global Kazkommerts Securities Inc.
"The government has really helped to put us in the market," he said. Karibzhanov said several major Kazakh enterprises were now contemplating issuing their own paper.

However, the western economist sounded a note of caution on how the bond would affect the republic's committment to stringent market economic reforms backed by the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank.
"If I were the president of the central bank, it would be a lot easier to issue a Eurobond than to go to the IMF," he said.
